newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Oil firm grits teeth in face of Colombian terror.
newsitem.headline: Oil firm grits teeth in face of Colombian terror.

text.p: They have been bombed out of their offices, seen their property sabotaged weekly and live in constant fear of being taken hostage, but employees of U.S. oil company Occidental Petroleum Corp are determined to stay in Colombia.
The chance of making a major new oil find in Colombia's Andean foothills is enough to keep the company living amid a climate of fear.
Over 30 people have been killed near its Cano Limon oilfield in eastern Colombia in the space of five days, marking a new low in a dirty guerilla war which has raged for more than three decades.
But even if Cano-Limon's production is now falling after 12 years, Colombia is still Occidental's third or fourth most important production area in the world.

"Production gives us a strategic advantage in exploration, we have prime acreage in the Llanos foothills, and the geographical position of the country makes it very important," said the company's communications chief Robert Stewart.
Last year, leftist guerillas blew up the pipeline that carries Cano Limon oil to the Caribbean coast 47 times. This year the number of attacks has already reached 38 and shows no signs of slowing.
"We have managed to make this very abnormal situation almost operate normally," Stewart said.
Workers for the state-owned oil company Ecopetrol have become expert pipeline repairers and managed to keep oil flowing at Cano Limon for over five years despite the repeated bombings.
But last week, Occidental was forced to shut in their oil wells after two consecutive bombings and intense guerilla activity prevented any swift patching.
When the army tried to recapture the zone, a helicopter was shot down, killing 20 soldiers and one civilian, and a ten more solders died in an ambush as they went in on foot.
"We haven't seen anything like this in years," Stewart added.
He thought the surge in bombings on the 730 kilometre (410 mile) pipeline could mark a prelude to peace talks, or a show of strength as elections approach next year.
But Occidental employees have forged a life in Colombia out of terror, and are not about to leave.
The company has already drilled one exploratory well in its newly acquired Laguna block and hopes soon to start exploring in the Samore block.

As if guerilla problems were not enough, Occidental was again thrust into the spotlight in Samore when indigenous U'wa indians took them to court, claiming the contract violated their ancestral rights to the province.

But the physical threat to the company was brought home most powerfully in 1988, when a car bomb exploded outside their downtown Bogota HQ. Projectiles from the bomb ripped through several floors of the building, bringing a new regime of fences, closed circuit television and airport-style security clearance.
"I'm the only member of my family that has stayed in Colombia. Maybe I have a suicidal streak," said Colombian-born Stewart.
